title: Asema, the Vampire of the Rainforest
summary: A vampire-like spirit from Surinamese folklore who sheds her skin at night and flies through the forest in search of blood.
full_text:
Deep in the rainforests of Suriname, where the canopy blocks out the stars and the howler monkeys scream at dawn, there is a creature that the Maroons fear above all others. The Asema is a woman by day, indistinguishable from any other. But by night, she sheds her skin like a snake, hanging it in her closet, and flies through the treetops as a ball of fire, searching for victims.

The Asema does not kill quickly. She returns night after night, drinking a little blood each time, leaving her victim weak and pale. The victim wastes away, unable to eat, unable to sleep, dreaming always of a red light approaching through the darkness. By the time the Asema has finished, there is nothing left but a shell, a body that breathes but no longer lives.

The only way to identify an Asema is to find her hidden skin. If you discover a woman's skin hanging in an unexpected place, you must sprinkle salt on it. When the Asema returns and finds her skin salted, she cannot re-enter it. She will be trapped in her spirit form, forced to wander the forest as a bodiless flame until dawn destroys her. It is a cruel fate, but the Maroons say it is the only way to stop her.

A man named Kwasi from the interior once suspected his wife of being an Asema. He followed her one night and saw her climb to the roof, where she removed her skin and flew away. Kwasi took the skin and rubbed it with pepper. When his wife returned, she could not re-enter her body. She cried and pleaded, but Kwasi was firm. At dawn, she dissolved into mist. Kwasi lived alone for the rest of his life, haunted by what he had done.

The Asema is a warning against trusting appearances. The kindest neighbor, the most loving wife, might be hiding a monstrous nature beneath her skin.
moral: The most dangerous monsters often wear familiar faces.

title: Didibri, the Rainbow Dragon
summary: A great dragon-like serpent associated with the rainbow, sometimes a bringer of destruction and other times a protector of hidden treasure.
full_text:
In the sky over Suriname, when the rain stops and the sun breaks through, a rainbow sometimes arches across the clouds. The old people of the interior do not point at it. They do not speak of it lightly. For the Didibri, the rainbow serpent, is watching. The Didibri is a creature of immense size, a serpent whose scales shimmer with all the colors of the rainbow. It lives in the deepest rivers and the highest clouds. When it moves through the water, it creates currents that can capsize boats. When it flies through the air, its passage is the rainbow.

The Didibri has two natures, like the rainbow itself, which is beautiful but also full of power. Sometimes it is a destroyer, a creature of chaos that uproots trees and floods villages. Other times it is a protector, guarding treasures hidden at the base of waterfalls or in caves behind the rainbows. The difference depends on how it is treated. Those who respect the Didibri, who do not stare too long at its colors, who leave offerings of gold dust at the river's edge, may find themselves blessed. But those who mock it, who try to capture it, who point and laugh will be swept away.

A group of gold prospectors once saw a Didibri in the Brokopondo region. Instead of showing respect, they fired their rifles at it, hoping to sell its scales. The Didibri vanished. That night, a storm unlike any seen in decades flattened their camp. The river rose thirty feet in an hour. Three men drowned. The survivors left the forest forever.

To this day, Surinamese children are taught never to point at a rainbow. The Didibri might see, and the Didibri might not forgive.
moral: Some beauty exists beyond human reach; let it be.

title: Bakru, the Forest Spirit Child
summary: A small, childlike forest spirit who can bring wealth to those who capture it but demands terrible sacrifices in return.
full_text:
The Bakru is one of the most feared spirits of the Surinamese forest. It appears as a small child, no more than three feet tall, with skin as black as coal and eyes that glow red in the darkness. It lives beneath the roots of giant kapok trees or in the hollow trunks of silk cotton trees. The Bakru is not evil by nature, but it is amoral, a creature that simply desires what it desires.

A person who captures a Bakru can force it to bring wealth. Gold, jewels, money, anything of value, the Bakru will fetch. But the price is unspeakable. The Bakru must be fed. Not with food, but with the life force of human beings. Every coin the Bakru brings must be paid for with a day of someone else's life. The owner of the Bakru will grow rich, but those around him will sicken and die without explanation.

A man named Hendrik from Paramaribo was desperate for money to pay his debts. He consulted a wiseman who told him how to capture a Bakru. Hendrik went into the forest at midnight, carrying a bottle of rum and a piece of red cloth. He found the Bakru's tree and set the trap. The spirit was caught. For a year, Hendrik prospered. His debts vanished. He built a new house. But his neighbors began to die. First the old, then the sick, then the young. Hendrik grew rich as his village grew empty. On the anniversary of the deal, the Bakru demanded more. Hendrik had no one left to sacrifice. The Bakru turned on him. Hendrik was found dead in his new house, his face frozen in terror, a single red cloth clutched in his hand.

The Bakru is still out there, in the forest, waiting for another desperate soul. Those who know the story leave the kapok trees undisturbed and count themselves lucky to be poor but alive.
moral: Wealth bought with suffering brings only ruin.
